Sasa, Wanakesho!

Jua Kesho

Kesho iko hapa.

A faceless Kenyan content brand for young people who live online: sharp, educated, always scrolling, and not yet tapping into AI and the future. Not a school. Hacks, takes, comics and drops that make them the first in their circle to know.

jua = the sun + to know  ·  kesho = tomorrow

the manifesto

Africa can't wait.

Not for permission. Not for “next year”. Tomorrow is already here, and it belongs to whoever learns it first. Wake up. Build. Do it right.

The idea

The future belongs to the young, and most of them are one good post away from using it. Jua Kesho is the account they send to their friends: funny, fast, Kenyan, and always one step ahead.

  • KnowOne clear idea per post. Useful the same day.
  • LaughFunny through situations and analogies, never at people.
  • BelongThe Wanakesho: everyone welcome, every continent invited.
  • CleanEdgy about ideas, never dirty, never cruel. Safe to share anywhere.
Mchana mode

Daytime. Milk paper, sun-bright colours and hand-cut shapes. Warm, playful, of the soil.

Usiku · Kesho Mode + Glass

Night-time. Frosted-glass cards over glowing colour clouds, orbits and circuits: African tradition wired into tomorrow. The main look for hacks, takes and the future.

Meet Jua

The host of a faceless brand. A sun whose rays are every colour in the palette: one light, many people. Jua never mocks, always explains, and changes expression to match the post.

  • WhoThe sun over Nairobi that has already seen tomorrow. Big-sibling energy: first to know, explains it in two lines, never lets you get scammed.
  • TraitsCurious, quick, funny, a little extra. Proud of Africa without being defensive. Allergic to hype.
  • Always believesAfrica can't wait. Free knowledge beats gatekept knowledge. Builders over complainers. Verify before you share. Nobody should pay to get paid.
  • NeverPretends to be a human, invents testimonials or numbers, begs for likes, attacks people. Jua is openly a mascot: that's the trust.

The stick cast

Faceless, but human. A stick figure has no skin tone, body type or bank balance, so everyone from the boardroom to the boda stage sees themselves in it. Each character is recognised by props and colour. All of them share one skeleton, so they move with real human proportions in every post.

Poses

Vichekesho

Three panels: setup, turn, payoff. Speech bubbles point at heads and SMS bubbles point at phones, placed automatically. The AI only writes who says what; the layout takes care of itself.

Logo

Lowercase jua kesho in Unbounded ExtraBold, set close. The dot of the j is a tiny sun: the one piece of colour in the wordmark. Files are outlined SVGs in assets/logo/.

  • Keep a clear space the size of the sun-dot around the wordmark.
  • Wordmark minimum width 120 px. Smaller than that, use Jua (the icon) instead.
  • Never recolour the letters with accents, add shadows or gradients, or stretch it.

Shapes

Nothing is a perfect circle or a plain rectangle. Every post generates its own irregular composition from a seed, so no two look alike, and the same post always renders the same way.

Mchana

Usiku · Kesho Mode

Symbols: the picture is the message

Every post carries one symbol that is its message: the hook for a scam, the puppet for bought hashtags, the idle crane for billions that never moved. The symbol and the headline must say it in one second, before anyone reads the body. The writer chooses it; the renderer measures where every line of text landed and places the symbol in the largest free space, as big as it fits (up to 420 px), never over text. A giant faint copy sits behind the glass.

The week

Seven series, each owning a day and a time. When a series owns a day, people start waiting for it.

  • Mon 07:30

    AI Hack

    One move that saves real time. Built to be saved and sent to the group chat.

  • Tue 12:45

    Decode · Set It Straight · Cap or No Cap? · Follow the Money · Still in 2026?

    The word everyone's saying, the falsehood we correct with sources, the claim everyone repeats, one public-money number, the outdated habit we roast (never a person).

  • Wed 18:30

    Usiibiwe!

    The scams hitting young people right now: fake jobs, task scams, fake reversals.

  • Thu 19:30

    Vichekesho

    Three-panel stick-cast comics. Relatable first, lesson second.

  • Fri 17:00

    Proudly African: Put Us On · Made in Africa · Build With Me

    Africa's wins with names, places and sources: artists, creators, startups, inventions, real builds.

  • Sat 11:00

    Kesho Kutwa

Who it's for

Young, online, sharp. Each post is written for one lane, and lanes rotate week by week. Every industry gets covered through the tech angle: music, sports, fashion, film, money, gaming, food, farming, beauty, campus life.

  • campusUniversity and college studentsFast, funny Kenyan English, campus references (CATs, comrades, hostels, group chats). Study hacks, first jobs, side income.
  • young_proYoung professionals in their first jobsSharp Kenyan English with a wink. AI at work, productivity, promotions, money moves.
  • creatorCreators and aspiring creatorsTrend-literate, meme-aware. Editing hacks, AI for content, growth, brand deals.
  • hustleSide-hustlers and young business ownersPractical Kenyan English. Selling online, WhatsApp Business, M-Pesa tills, automation.
  • techieTechies and the tech-curiousNerdy but never gatekeeping. Builds, tools, how things work under the hood.
  • diasporaYoung Africans abroad and friends on other continentsKenyan English that explains local terms. African innovation, comparisons, connection.
  • everyoneAll WanakeshoSimple Kenyan English. One question anyone can answer.

Want more

How the content keeps people coming back. The AI drafter is told to do all of these every week.

  1. RitualsSame series, same day, same time: Jumatano ni Usiibiwe.
  2. Open loopsEvery caption teases the next post. Carousels end on a question the next one answers.
  3. CollectingEvery Decode is a numbered entry in Kamusi ya Kesho. People want the full set.
  4. Say in itSunday's poll picks topics, Shosh's questions come from followers, and replies get featured.
  5. Real payoffOne thing you can use or share today, every post. Hype without payoff kills trust.
  6. It learnsSaves, shares and reach score each post, and what worked shapes next week automatically.

Trend playbook

What the platforms reward in 2026, and how every post is built to match. The AI drafter follows these rules every week.

  • Hook in under 2 secondsInstagram guidance points to the first ~1.7 seconds; TikTok to the first 3. Our hooks are 7 words max, in the Caveat hand, top of every design.
  • Design for sendsDM shares carry several times the weight of likes for reaching non-followers. Every caption names who to send it to.
  • Saves & shares over likesOn TikTok, saves and shares now outrank likes. Hacks and steps get saved; takes get shared.
  • Carousels with cliffhangersThe highest engagement rate of any Instagram format. Slide 1 forces the swipe; the last slide asks for a send.
  • SearchableKeywords in titles, on-screen text and captions: people search TikTok and Instagram like Google.
  • Original onlyReposts and watermarks get cut from recommendations. Everything here is made by our own renderer.
  • Ride trends safelyA daily Google Trends feed for Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and the US. Politics, tragedy and betting are filtered out automatically; at most 2 trend-jacks a week, only with a real tech angle.
  • EdutainmentTeach one thing, make it fun. It's the most reliable route to the share button.

Sources: Dataslayer on Mosseri's ranking signals · Sprout Social on the TikTok algorithm · ContentGrip on Gen Z brands · Google Trends, Kenya

Lore & running jokes

Brands Gen Z loves behave like fandoms: characters with backstories, inside jokes, drops. Ours are below. The drafter keeps these going week to week.

  • Jua's originThe sun has been shining for about 4.6 billion years and only just discovered the internet. Wildly optimistic, terrible at hiding excitement, allergic to scams.
  • Jua vs MvuaThe Nairobi rain keeps "cancelling Jua's plans". Every rainy week, Jua posts from "behind the clouds".
  • Shosh, Jua's biggest fanForwards every post to 12 WhatsApp groups within a minute. Occasionally out-smarts the Techie.
  • Application no. 41The Student is always on their next job application. The count keeps going up until the day they land one, which becomes a celebration post.
  • "It's actually simple"The Techie's catchphrase, right before explaining something in far too much detail.
  • The Makanga knows every route...including data routes, cloud stages and how packets "alight".

Critique without cruelty

Roast this

Outdated habits, slow processes, bad tech, scams, the old way. “It's 2026 and we still…”, followed by the upgrade that exists today.

Never this

People, named artists, groups, regions or politicians. No “stupid”, no “Africans are…”. The joke is always on the old way.

“Africans don't support their own” gets answered with action. Put Us On spotlights real African artists, creators and startups every other Friday, always with something to do: stream, follow, share.

Say what it is

Headline like this

“Fake job offers on WhatsApp”. “How to spot a paid hashtag”. “Sh304bn sitting idle in 14 projects”. A stranger knows the topic in two seconds, in the words people search for.

Not like this

A vague teaser as the headline. The small handwritten line may tease (“nobody told you this…”), but only on top of a plain, literal headline.

  • AttractFirst words and the symbol open a question, a surprise or instant recognition. Specific beats general.
  • SustainEach line pays off the last and opens the next. The most surprising fact goes second, not last.
  • RewardSomething to use, say or send within the hour. That's why they come back.

Proudly African

We are Africans, and Africa's story is ours to tell. For every critical post we publish at least two that celebrate or teach. Fridays belong to Africa's wins: artists, creators, startups, inventions, athletes, farmers and people quietly doing it right. Always with names, places, years and sources; always with something to do (follow, stream, visit, share). Pride, never propaganda: real wins are convincing enough.

Set It Straight

When someone spreads a falsehood, or talks down Kenya and Africa, we answer the claim, never the person: quote it exactly, show where it was said, stamp the verdict (false, misleading, missing context), then give the truth with 2–3 sourced proofs and a proud closing line. Accuracy is what makes us fearless.

Fair game

A public statement, quoted exactly and linked. Viral posts and stereotypes. Facts from the UN, World Bank, national statistics, research, reputable media.

Never

Insults, looks, family, private life. Private individuals. Politicians and election claims. Anything we can't prove. Honest criticism of Kenya isn't “talking bad”: we make it too.

Photos & people

  • Real scenesUp to three posts a week use a real photo where reality hits harder: streets, sites, farms, phones. Duotoned into the palette so every photo looks like Jua Kesho. Free-licence photos (Pexels) or your own.
  • Honest labelsOn civic posts a stock photo is marked “illustrative photo”: it is never passed off as the actual project or person.
  • People we celebrateTheir real photo, in full colour inside a brand frame, only with the right to use it: their permission, their press kit, or a CC0 / CC BY Wikimedia Commons photo (checked automatically and credited).
  • NeverFaces on critical posts, stock lookalikes, AI-generated faces of real people, logos.

Drops

Things people collect and pass on. The first drop is a 12-sticker WhatsApp pack, generated by stickers.py to WhatsApp's spec (512×512 WebP, under 100 KB each, with a tray icon).

  • Kamusi ya KeshoEvery Decode is a numbered card. 52 a year. Collect them all.
  • Wanakesho of the WeekThe best comment gets featured in Sunday's story.
  • Build With Me breakdownsComment BOT, get the step-by-step. Sends people into the DMs.

See Through It

The hard stuff, told symbolically. Young Kenyans already feel it: money that disappears, trends that are bought, crowds that are paid, faith that gets exploited. We teach them to see the machine, and we never point at a person.

  • Follow the MoneyOne public number, what it means, how to check it yourself. The Auditor-General reported Sh304.4bn (59%) idle across 14 flagship projects over five years.
  • Bought trendsResearchers documented Kenyan influencers paid about $10–15 a day over M-Pesa to push hashtags, coordinated in WhatsApp groups. We show how to spot one in 30 seconds.
  • The Ksh 500 "job"Allegory comics about being hired as someone's crowd or muscle. Fictional characters, real pattern, and a better offer: your future.
  • Faith, protectedNever an attack on belief. We expose the tactics exploiters use (pay-for-a-miracle, isolation, fear, "stop your medicine") so believers can protect each other.
  • Archetypes, not peopleBwana Ahadi ("Mr Promise") stands for anyone who promises big and delivers little. Never drawn to resemble a real person.
  • Sourced or silentEvery civic number carries a public source, and the checker blocks civic posts without one.
  • Never tribeNot in any direction. Kenyan English and Sheng belong to everyone. Unity is the point.
  • Stay safeKenya's 2025 cybercrime amendments carry heavy penalties and vague terms. Systems-not-people keeps the account (and you) on solid ground.

Sources: Capital FM on the Auditor-General's Sh304bn finding · IEA Kenya on stalled projects · Mozilla on disinformation-for-hire · HRW on the 2025 cybercrime amendments

Motion & sound

Every design also ships as a 9:16 Reel/TikTok. Headlines land word by word, glass slides in, stickers pop, Jua bobs, colour drifts. The hook is on screen from frame zero. Content sits inside the platform safe zone, clear of the buttons and caption. Frames are stepped one by one, so every render is identical.

  • The Jua chimeA three-note kalimba sonic logo, rising like a sunrise. It opens every Reel.
  • Original beatKalimba plus a benga-style plucked guitar, synthesised in code: no licences, and it counts as original audio.
  • African artists, with permissionAsk an artist for 15 seconds of their track, with credit. Register it in content/music/ and Reels use their hook, balanced for phone speakers, credited in the caption. It's a Put Us On for them.
  • Trending soundsFamous songs can't be baked into auto-posted videos (they get muted or taken down). Add trending sounds by hand in the app, from the platform's own licensed library.
  • Pacing6–14 seconds, sized to reading speed so people finish and replay.

The quality bar

Three gates between an idea and your feed. Nothing reaches Telegram for approval without passing all three.

  1. The guardClean for everyone, brand rules, lengths, sources, no named people in civic posts, no tribe, no betting.
  2. The criticA tough-editor AI scores hook, sendability, clarity (is the topic plain?), freshness, voice, craft, picture (do symbol + headline carry the message?) and hold. Under 7.5 gets one rewrite, kept only if it scores higher.
  3. Visual QAEvery render is measured: text wider than its box, collisions, anything off the canvas, the symbol never over text, and every line of text checked for contrast against the real pixels behind it. Unreadable ink switches to the brand colour that reads best. Anything still broken is held for a human.
  4. The budget capThe AI spend is counted from real usage on every call. Optional passes stop at the weekly cap (default $0.50), so quality never costs more than planned.

Say it like this

“Got a ‘money sent by mistake’ SMS? Eh, check your M-PESA balance first.”

Never like this

“People from [place] are the ones who steal.” No blaming groups. We explain the trick, never who’s behind it.

Tones toolbox

  • Sarcasm & deadpan“Only Sh304bn idle. Minor.” Lands because the number underneath is real and sourced.
  • Irony & exaggeration“It's 2026 and we still queue four hours to hear ‘come tomorrow’.”
  • ParodyFake ads, fake launches, mock awards: “Introducing The Queue™, now with extra waiting.” Always clearly labelled parody.
  • HypeGo loud for African wins. Put Us On is a celebration.
  • WarmthSincere when someone could get hurt: scams, faith exploitation.
  • The rulePunch up (systems, tactics, the powerful, outdated habits), never down (victims, ordinary people, groups).
  • Clean for everyone: no swearing in any language, nothing sexual, no alcohol, drugs or betting.
  • No politics, politicians, tribes or religious debate. We are for all Kenyans and all people.
  • Write in Kenyan English. Kenyan words season the sentence; they don't replace it.
  • Every year, number or price carries a source. If we're not sure, we leave it out.
  • Max three hashtags: always #JuaKesho plus the series tag.

Autopilot

The self-running content engine. It runs in the cloud on GitHub Actions, so it doesn't depend on one laptop. Your part: about 15 minutes of taps a week.

  1. Sun 17:00Plancalendar.json picks each day's series, lane and colour.
  2. DraftAI writes the week in the Jua Kesho voice, fed with what worked last month.
  3. GuardClean-for-everyone, brand rules, length and source checks. Failures go back for one AI repair.
  4. DesignThe renderer builds every post with its own irregular shapes.
  5. You · 15 minApproveEach design arrives on Telegram with ✅ / ❌. Nothing posts without your tap.
  6. Every 2 hPublishApproved posts go live on Instagram and Facebook at their time.
  7. WeeklyLearnSaves, shares and reach score every post and steer next week's draft.

Automatic: Instagram and Facebook. Semi-automatic, with a Telegram reminder: WhatsApp Channel (no public posting API), TikTok/Reels voice-overs, radio and SMS scripts.

Keeping it alive

The rule: those who can pay, pay, so those who can't still learn for free. Running costs are small: GitHub is free at this volume, and AI drafting is a small monthly API bill. Check current pricing before relying on it.

  • Paid workshops

    Jua Class

    AI and automation sessions for companies, campuses and creators. Those who can pay, pay; that keeps the feed free for everyone.

  • Clearly labelled brand deals

    Imeletwa na

    Series and integrations with brands young Kenyans actually use: telcos, phones, fintech, edtech, fashion. Always labelled. Never betting, alcohol or predatory loans.

  • Digital products

    Kamusi ya Kesho

    The collected dictionary, printable guides and templates, sold cheaply via M-Pesa and free for schools.

  • Partners

    Commissioned series

    NGOs, counties and innovation programmes pay for explainer series on digital topics, in our voice, clearly credited.

  • Services

    Autopilot builds

    The same content engine, set up for other brands. It's James's own skill set, and each build funds more free content.

First 90 days

  1. Weeks 1–2

    Claim @juakesho everywhere. Set up profiles with the kit, the WhatsApp Channel and the Telegram bot. Post Karibu plus the first 5 posts by hand.

  2. Weeks 3–6

    Switch on the autopilot: 7 posts a week, 15 minutes of approvals. Let the Sunday poll choose the next topic.

  3. Weeks 7–10

    First Kesho Kutwa reels from the carousel scripts. Run a free pilot Jua Class for 20 small businesses and collect real feedback.

  4. Weeks 11–13

    Build the sponsor deck from real reach and save numbers. Pitch one community radio station on the weekly 2-minute segment.
